builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Evolution Under Fire: Evolving Agent Safety Harnesses with Adaptive Injection Stressors
summary: The method replaces manual, static design of safety harnesses for tool-using agents with automated evolutionary search that optimizes executable harness code against utility and attack-success objectives. It costs significant inference compute for the tree-search evolution loop (using API models or a local evaluator model) plus engineering effort to set up benchmarks, evaluators, and stressor evolution, and it adds a harness layer that affects runtime behavior. It can fail through overfitting to the specific benchmark and attack distribution, degraded protection on harder benchmarks (attack success remains 62.0% on Agent-SafetyBench), regression under adaptive attackers who evolve against the fixed harness, and utility loss if the harness blocks legitimate instructions.
rationale: Automated harness evolution targets exactly the prompt-injection threat the reader faces in production, but its benefits are benchmark-dependent and the evolution pipeline's compute and engineering cost requires a small-scale pilot before adoption.
technique: Evolutionary search for agent safety harnesses

claims.statement: The method replaces manual, static design of safety harnesses for tool-using agents with automated evolutionary search that optimizes executable harness code against utility and attack-success objectives. It costs significant inference compute for the tree-search evolution loop (using API models or a local evaluator model) plus engineering effort to set up benchmarks, evaluators, and stressor evolution, and it adds a harness layer that affects runtime behavior. It can fail through overfitting to the specific benchmark and attack distribution, degraded protection on harder benchmarks (attack success remains 62.0% on Agent-SafetyBench), regression under adaptive attackers who evolve against the fixed harness, and utility loss if the harness blocks legitimate instructions.

On AgentDyn with GPT-4o-mini, the evolved harness reduces attack success from 50.4% to 3.0% (a 16.8x reduction) while improving utility; transfer to another model reduces attack success from 32.1% to 0.9%.
